analysis.one_liner: Raises tobacco taxes sharply and spends the money on children's health and anti-smoking programs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan tobacco tax bill with one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal excise tax on cigarettes roughly eightfold by 2002 — from about 24 cents a pack to about $1.89 — along with big increases on cigars, smokeless tobacco, and pipe tobacco. The money would have gone into a dedicated trust fund: three-quarters to states for smoking prevention, cessation, children's health insurance, and nutrition programs for women and infants, and one-quarter to federal health agencies plus compensation for tobacco farming communities. It also would have let states require their own health warnings on cigarette ads, and urged that any final tobacco law include FDA regulation and penalties for marketing to children.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and children gain through expanded children's health insurance, WIC nutrition aid, and maternal health grants; smokers trying to quit gain through funded cessation programs; states gain flexible public health money; and tobacco farming families gain transition compensation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children's health programs and anti-smoking efforts

how_it_helps.text: Sets cigarette tax at $37 per thousand in 1999, $67 in 2000, $92 in 2001, and $94.50 in 2002 — roughly $1.89 per pack, up from about 24 cents — with similar jumps for other tobacco products [S3].

Requires 75% of the new revenue go to states for tobacco education and prevention, cessation services, the Children's Health Insurance Program, WIC or maternal and child health block grants, and community tobacco control programs [S3].
Sends 25% to federal programs including FDA tobacco control, compensation to protect tobacco farming families and communities, NIH research, and CDC smoking-reduction work [S3].
Repeals the federal provision that limits health-related statements on cigarette and smokeless tobacco advertising, freeing states and manufacturers to communicate health risks [S2].

Expresses the sense of the House that any final tobacco law funded by the trust fund must include FDA authority to regulate tobacco, penalties for advertising that targets children, secondhand-smoke limits, and disclosure of industry documents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers pay through much higher prices — the tax rises roughly eightfold on cigarettes in five years, and excise taxes fall hardest on lower-income smokers who smoke at higher rates. Tobacco companies pay the tax directly and face a floor-stocks tax on inventory, new penalties on export-labeled products resold domestically, and state-level advertising rules.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes are regressive: lower-income smokers pay the largest share of the tax relative to income, and the bill imposes the increases in steep annual steps [S3].
Section 102 allows a business tax deduction for the portion of the new excise taxes above 1998 rates, softening the cost to companies rather than to consumers [S3].

Title IV is only a non-binding statement of the House's views; the bill itself does not create FDA authority, child-marketing penalties, or secondhand-smoke rules — it merely says any later law should [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health payoff would have been large — new funding for children's insurance, nutrition, and quitting programs paid by tobacco use itself, which also discourages smoking, especially among price-sensitive teens. The honest cost is that the tax burden falls on smokers, disproportionately lower-income ones, and the near-eightfold rate increase in four years would hit them abruptly. The bill's regulatory ambitions are largely aspirational, resting in a non-binding title. On balance it is a well-aimed public health bill whose main design flaw is its regressivity.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two committees on the day it was introduced, forwarded to a Commerce subcommittee a week later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Hansen (R-UT) introduced the bill on October 29, 1997, for himself and Rep. Martin Meehan, a Democrat, making it a bipartisan sponsorship [S3].
It was referred the same day to both the Ways and Means Committee, which handles taxes, and the Commerce Committee [S5].
On November 9, 1997, the Commerce Committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill had only one cosponsor [S4] and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies and their marketers: cigarette taxes stayed at the lower rates already scheduled in the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, no advertising restrictions or FDA authority was enacted, and the bill's public health funding never materialized.

for.name: James V. Hansen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored the tobacco tax increase and trust fund.

for.name: Martin Meehan
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further recorded action on it.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley
against.what_they_did: His committee held the bill's health provisions; it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on November 9, 1997, and never reported out.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Ran a major lobbying and advertising campaign in 1997-98 against tobacco tax and regulation legislation generally.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor, but because no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill raises cigarette excise taxes roughly eightfold by 2002, adds floor-stocks taxes on existing inventory, tightens export/import rules with new penalties, and lets states impose their own health warnings. Tobacco companies benefit from the bill's failure, which left rates at the much lower scheduled levels.

Repealing the federal limits on health-related statements in tobacco advertising opens the door to state advertising rules, and the bill urges stiff penalties for advertising aimed at children. Its defeat preserved the existing marketing framework.
A quarter of the federal share of the trust fund would protect the financial well-being of tobacco farming families and communities, cushioning them as tobacco use declines.
